title: Where Does a City of 281 Million For-Hire Trips Actually Concentrate?
tagline: A scroll-driven atlas of 280,236,580 cleaned New York for-hire trips from 2024 (yellow, green and high-volume FHV), told as one ring of 263 taxi zones that becomes a map, a congestion indicator, a labeled BPR scenario lab and a plain account of how we know.
note: Trip data is from the NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission, which states it did not create the data and makes no representation as to its accuracy. Weather is NOAA GHCN-Daily, station USW00094728 (Central Park), applied citywide. Locations are taxi zones, not coordinates, so no route or trajectory is shown. The scenario lab is SIMULATED; the weather result is an association, not a cause. Cells with fewer than 11 trips are suppressed.
problem:
New York publishes every taxi and app-based car trip as a row, and the files are too big and too messy to read directly: 281,300,386 rows for 2024, about a million of them excluded as invalid (negative durations, trips over 80 mph and similar). The practical question is how for-hire demand moves across the 263 taxi zones through the week, and how sensitive the city's pace is to changes in demand.

The constraint that shapes everything: the data holds zone IDs, not coordinates or paths. Any picture of "routes" would be invented, so the site draws zone-to-zone relationships and says so.
built:
An offline pipeline and a static site joined by a contract.

  • Pipeline: checksummed ingestion of 36 trip files, a DuckDB cleaner with six ordered exclusion rules so that raw rows equal kept rows plus exclusions per service-month, zone and aggregate modeling, and a publisher that writes 17 JSON artifacts with a JSON Schema each.
  • Analytics: a congestion indicator (median speed against each zone's own overnight free flow), a flow-weighted network, k-means zone clusters, a weather regression with HAC errors, and a BPR scenario model with held-out validation.
  • Site: one Canvas 2D ring carried from the opening through the rush hour and corridors, morphing into a deck.gl map, then a scenario lab, an observed-versus-simulated comparison and an evidence chapter.

Every figure on the page carries an honesty tag: OBSERVED, DERIVED, PREDICTED or SIMULATED.

steps.title: Make the count add up before drawing anything
steps.body: Each raw row gets exactly one outcome: the first failing rule, otherwise kept. The ledger reconciles to the row: 281,300,386 raw rows, 280,236,580 kept, 1,063,806 excluded (0.38%). Yellow loses 2.33% and green 6.81%, high-volume FHV 0.02%. A test asserts the identity per service-month, and a slower test re-counts the raw Parquet.

steps.title: Say what the data cannot show
steps.body: There are no coordinates after 2016, so there are no routes. Origin-destination pairs are zone to zone. The busiest directed pair is Upper East Side South to Upper East Side North (387,897 trips); including trips that start and end in the same zone, zone 76 within itself leads with 778,346.

steps.title: A congestion indicator with a stated proxy
steps.body: Free flow is the 85th percentile of a zone's overnight hour-of-week median speeds; the indicator is median speed divided by that. At the weekday AM peak, Manhattan runs at 47.6% of its free-flow speed (10.2 of 21.3 mph) and Staten Island at 72.2%. It is a for-hire proxy, not road speed, and the free-flow definition is varied in a robustness table.

steps.title: Report the weak clusters as weak
steps.body: Zones are clustered by the shape of their week. Silhouette is highest at the smallest allowed k: k = 3 scores 0.333, k = 4 scores 0.305. The site reports a coarse three-type typology (stability ARI mean 0.966; random labels score 0.006 or less) rather than forcing more.

steps.title: Rain is an association
steps.body: Daily log trips regressed on precipitation, snow, temperature, day of week, month and holidays with Newey-West errors: each additional 10 mm of rain goes with 2.00% more daily trips (95% CI 1.15% to 2.86%). One station, no event controls, so the page does not claim a mechanism.

steps.title: A scenario model that is labeled SIMULATED
steps.body: A BPR volume-delay curve is fitted per borough to hour-of-week volume and pace. Capacity is fixed to the busiest-5% hourly volume, a normalization rather than engineered capacity, so that alpha is identified. Parameters from January to September are scored on October to December and beat both constant baselines. Fitted beta is near 1 and R-squared is moderate (0.50 to 0.79), so the lab flags anything beyond observed volume as extrapolation.

steps.title: Suppress small cells, state the count
steps.body: Any published count of 1 to 10 trips becomes null. 25,018 trips in OD pairs under 11 annual trips are withheld from the OD totals; headline shares are computed before suppression and the artifact says so.

results:
Data. 280,236,580 kept trips; 85.4% high-volume FHV, 14.3% yellow, 0.2% green; mean 532 trips a minute. 50 of 263 zones account for half of all known-zone pickups. Weekday peaks are 8 AM and 6 PM. At the weekday AM peak Manhattan runs at 47.6% of its free-flow speed (10.2 of 21.3 mph). LaGuardia is the highest-betweenness zone.

Checks. 50 pytest tests (49 without the raw-data re-count), 70 Vitest tests and 242 Playwright tests pass with 0 failed and 0 flaky (QA ran them with one worker); TypeScript and lint are clean. axe-core found 0 violations in 160 scans (10 scenes, normal and reduced motion, at 1440, 1024, 1024 with classic scrollbars and 390 wide). Lighthouse on the live GitHub Pages site, three runs on a busy laptop (1-minute load about 11): mobile performance 0.98 to 0.99, largest contentful paint 1.66 to 2.18 s, layout shift 0, accessibility 1.0, best practices 1.0; desktop performance 1.0 in all three runs, largest contentful paint 0.38 to 0.45 s. Frame pacing (earlier QA pass, laptop, software WebGL): 95th-percentile frame 10.7 ms on desktop and 28.3 ms at 390x844 with the CPU throttled 4x, about 35 fps. That is not a real phone.

Independent QA. A reviewer who did not build the site read contact sheets and ran its own probes over seven passes. The first found 7 major defects; later passes found fewer (a layout-class bug from the wrong viewport width, a footer credit under the fixed navigation at 1280x720, labels colliding with the ring dial) until pass 7 passed with none open.

Known limitations. Scene data is 887 KB gzipped against a 400 KB budget (it loads per scene). At 1024 px wide the closing footer is crossed by a decorative chord. Two timing minors remain: a 13 px title settle at 768 px wide with classic scrollbars, and one frame of stale labels when the congestion metric is switched. The data is for-hire trips only, zone-level (no routes), one year and one weather station.
